name: Audit Trails and Explainability
question: Can we show exactly why the agent decided what it did?
summary: An audit trail records, for every decision, what the agent saw, which model and prompt versions ran, which rules and documents it used, which tools it called, what it decided with reason codes, and who reviewed or overrode it. Records go to append-only storage with hash chaining or write-once retention so tampering is detectable, with personal data masked or tokenised, and kept for the legal retention period. Explainability for agents means reason codes and a replayable trace, not just a feature-importance chart.
useCases: Any decision a customer or regulator can challenge
steps: Define the questions an auditor will ask about a decision
Log the fields that answer each question, with versions
Write to append-only, hash-chained or write-once storage
Mask personal data and set retention to the legal period
pitfalls: Logs editable by the team being audited
Raw Aadhaar or PAN numbers in logs
tools: Object storage with write-once retention (S3 Object Lock or equivalent)
SHAP or reason codes for scored models
remember: Every decision replayable, every record tamper-evident, no raw personal data.
caption: Retention periods vary by rule; KYC records are commonly kept five years after the relationship ends.

code.text: def record(self, case_id, doc_bytes, fields, run, decision, reasons, reviewer):
"fields": mask_pii(fields),          # no raw Aadhaar or PAN
return all(e["prev"] == p["hash"] for p, e in zip(entries, entries[1:]))
# retention: longest legal period that applies

steps.title: What did it see?
steps.text: A hash of the uploaded document proves which file was read without storing it twice; the extracted fields show what the agent took from it.

steps.title: Which system was it?
steps.text: Model and prompt versions. Without them, a replay cannot tell whether a later change caused the decision.

steps.title: Why, and who?
steps.text: The policy clauses used, the tool calls and results, reason codes, and the reviewer. The disputed rejection turned out to be an address mismatch under a named clause.

steps.title: Make edits detectable
steps.text: Each record carries the previous record’s hash and goes to write-once storage. Changing or deleting any record breaks the chain.

steps.title: No raw personal data
steps.text: Mask identifiers in the log. The audit trail must not become the biggest store of Aadhaar numbers in the company.

steps.title: Keep it long enough
steps.text: Timestamps, and retention set to the longest legal requirement; KYC records are commonly kept five years after the relationship ends.

Keep them long enough without raw personal data

practice.scenario: A customer of a fictional broker complained through SEBI’s SCORES portal that the KYC agent had rejected their account for no reason. The firm’s logs held only “rejected” and a timestamp, so it could not show what the agent had seen or which rule it had applied. It now writes a hash-chained record for every decision: the document hash, extracted fields with Aadhaar masked, model and prompt versions, policy clauses used, tool results, reason codes and the reviewer. A replay showed an address mismatch, and the complaint was answered with evidence.

industries.use: KYC decisions that customers can escalate to SEBI
Credit decisions that need reason codes
Claim rejections reviewed by an ombudsman

practice.analogy: An aircraft’s flight recorder: it records enough to reconstruct what happened, it is built so nobody can quietly edit it, and it is read after something goes wrong.

library.name: OpenTelemetry + write-once storage
library.what: GenAI semantic conventions capture each model and tool call as spans; decision records go to object storage with write-once retention, such as S3 Object Lock.

practice.note: Set retention to the longest legal requirement that applies. KYC records are commonly kept for five years after the relationship ends; confirm with compliance.

numericDrill.question: A broker’s KYC agent makes 3 million decisions a year. Each hash-chained decision record is 4 KB, and records are kept for 5 years. How much storage do the retained records need, in GB? (Use 1 GB = 1,000,000 KB.)
numericDrill.answer: 3,000,000 × 4 KB = 12 GB a year; over 5 years, 60 GB. That is small compared with the cost of being unable to explain one disputed decision; the design constraint is completeness and tamper evidence, not storage.

interview.question: What should an audit record for an AI decision contain?
interview.answer: Enough to replay the decision: a hash of the input and the extracted fields with personal data masked, the model and prompt versions, the documents and policy clauses used, tool calls and results, the decision and reason codes, the human reviewer and any override with its reason, and timestamps. Records should be append-only and tamper-evident.

interview.question: How do you make LLM decisions explainable to a regulator?
interview.answer: Constrain the agent to produce structured reason codes tied to written policy clauses, log the evidence each code rests on, and keep a replayable trace with versions. For scored models, feature attributions such as SHAP can support the reason codes. A post-hoc narrative written by the model alone is not an explanation.

mistakes.fix: Log inputs, versions, grounds, actions and people
Append-only storage with hash chaining or write-once retention
